::: {.lead}
*Harbor Guard* is a tower-defence game for phones. Ships sail into a harbour,
and the player builds towers to stop them. Before the game can draw one
picture, it must know many things as numbers: Where is each ship? Where is
each tower? How high is the tower? In this lesson you learn why games need
mathematics, and how a **coordinate system** turns the question "where is
it?" into numbers. We start with one number on a line, then two numbers on a
flat level, then three numbers in a 3D world. Every section ends with a short
task: on paper, in the free tool GeoGebra or in a mini-game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop frame-rate coordinate-system origin axis coordinate ordered-pair quadrant handedness >}}

## 1.1 Mathematics in game development

For a computer, a game is a set of numbers in memory: the positions of the
characters, their health, the score, the time left. The game program repeats
three steps again and again:

1. read the player's input (a tap, a swipe, a button);
2. change the numbers by the rules of the game;
3. draw a picture of the game on the screen.

These three steps are the **game loop**. One pass through the loop makes one
picture, called a **frame** (@fig-game-loop).

![The game loop. One pass makes one frame.](images/game-loop.png){#fig-game-loop width=78%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Frame rate"}
The **frame rate** is the number of frames a game makes in one second. It is
written in frames per second (fps). Most phone games run at 30 or 60 fps.
:::

So the game loop runs very fast: at 60 fps it runs 60 times every second.
All the work for one frame must be done in that short time. This is why game
mathematics uses simple steps: a few additions and multiplications for each
object, in every frame.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — How often does the loop run?"}
A racing game runs at 60 fps.

1. In one second, the loop runs 60 times.
2. In 10 seconds, it runs $10 \times 60 = 600$ times.
3. So the game updates the position of every car 600 times in 10 seconds.
   If the game is slower, at 30 fps, it updates them only 300 times, and the
   cars move less smoothly.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — One tap, one pass of the loop"}
In *Harbor Guard*, the player taps an empty place to build a tower.

1. **Read the input:** the game reads where the finger touched.
2. **Change the numbers:** the game adds a tower at that place and takes 50
   coins from the player: coins go from 200 to 150.
3. **Draw:** the next frame shows the new tower and the number 150.
4. All this happens in one pass of the loop. The player sees the tower in the
   very next frame.
:::

Mathematics is everywhere in a game. @tbl-map shows where the topics of this
course appear.

| What the game does | Mathematics | Weeks |
|---|---|---|
| Know where every object is; move it | coordinates, vectors | 1–3 |
| Aim a turret; make an object bob up and down | trigonometry | 4 |
| Move, turn and resize models | matrices | 5–7 |
| Decide if a door opens or an enemy attacks | logic | 9–10 |
| Make loot, critical hits and random levels | probability | 11–13 |

: Mathematics behind common game tasks. {#tbl-map}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — The mathematics of Harbor Guard"}
Four things that *Harbor Guard* must compute, and the mathematics behind
them:

1. Where each ship is, in every frame: **coordinates**.
2. How the ship moves towards the harbour: **vectors**.
3. Where a tower must turn to aim at a ship: **trigonometry**.
4. If a ship drops a rare reward: **probability**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the mathematics in a game"}
Play a game on your phone for two minutes.

1. Write four things that the game must compute with numbers, for example
   "the position of my car" or "the chance of a rare item".
2. For each one, write the mathematics from @tbl-map that it needs.

*Your result:* a table with four rows: game thing, mathematics.
:::

## 1.2 One-dimensional coordinates

The simplest coordinate system is the **number line**. We choose one point,
the **origin**, and call it 0. We choose a unit of length, for example one
metre, and a positive direction, for example to the right. Then every point
on the line has one number, its **coordinate**: how many units it is from the
origin. Points on the right have positive coordinates. Points on the left
have negative coordinates.

![A one-dimensional world: a runner game. The position along the track is one number, x.](images/number-line.png){#fig-number-line width=88%}

A runner game is a good example. The character runs along a track, so one
number is enough to say where it is (@fig-number-line). In a board game, the
positions are whole numbers: a piece is on square 3 or on square 4, never
between. In a running game, a position can also be a decimal number, such as
3.5.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — Displacement and distance on a line"}
An object moves from a start coordinate to an end coordinate. Its
**displacement** is *end minus start*. The sign shows the direction: plus
means to the right, minus means to the left. The **distance** is the size of
the displacement without its sign. A distance is never negative.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.4 — Back to the checkpoint"}
In the runner game of @fig-number-line, the player is at 4. The last
checkpoint is at $-3$. The player falls and goes back to the checkpoint.

1. Displacement: end minus start $= -3 - 4 = -7$. The minus sign means that
   the player moves to the left.
2. Distance: 7 units.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Mixing up displacement and distance. A displacement of $-7$ and a
displacement of $+7$ have the same distance: 7 units. A negative distance is
always an error.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A runner track on paper"}
1. Draw a number line from $-5$ to $10$.
2. Mark the start at 0, a coin at 6 and a trap at $-2$.
3. The player runs from the start to the coin, then falls back to the trap.
   Write the displacement and the distance of each move.

*Your result:* the drawing, two displacements and two distances.
:::

## 1.3 Two-dimensional coordinates

A two-dimensional (2D) game world, such as a platform game or a map, needs
two numbers for each point. The **Cartesian coordinate system** uses two
number lines that cross at the origin at a right angle (@fig-quadrants):

- the horizontal line is the **x-axis**; $x$ grows to the right;
- the vertical line is the **y-axis**; $y$ grows upward.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.3 — Ordered pair"}
A point in the plane is written as an **ordered pair** $(x, y)$. The first
number is the $x$-coordinate (left–right). The second number is the
$y$-coordinate (down–up). The order matters: $(3, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$ are
different points.
:::

The two axes cut the plane into four parts, the **quadrants**, numbered I to
IV, starting at the top right and going anticlockwise. The signs of the two
coordinates tell the quadrant (@tbl-quadrants). A point with a zero
coordinate lies on an axis, not in a quadrant.

![The four quadrants and their signs, with four game objects in a 2D level.](images/quadrants.png){#fig-quadrants width=58%}

| Quadrant | Sign of x | Sign of y | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | + | + | (4, 3) |
| II | − | + | (−3, 2) |
| III | − | − | (−4, −2) |
| IV | + | − | (2, −3) |

: Signs of the four quadrants. {#tbl-quadrants}

Level designers often put the origin in the centre of a level, or where the
player starts. Then negative numbers are normal: an enemy at $(-6, 1)$ is six
units to the left of the centre and one unit up.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.5 — Reading positions in a level"}
In @fig-quadrants, the coin is at $(4, 3)$, the key at $(-3, 2)$ and the exit
at $(2, -3)$.

1. The coin: $x$ is plus, $y$ is plus → quadrant I. It is right of the centre
   and up.
2. The key: $x$ is minus, $y$ is plus → quadrant II. It is left and up.
3. The exit: $x$ is plus, $y$ is minus → quadrant IV. It is right and down.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.6 — Placing an object"}
A designer wants a tree 5 units to the left of the centre, on the ground line
of the level ($y = 0$).

1. Left means a negative $x$: $x = -5$.
2. On the ground line: $y = 0$.
3. The tree is at $(-5, 0)$. It is on the x-axis, so it is in no quadrant.
:::

Moving on a 2D level is like moving on two number lines at the same time:
one move changes $x$ (left–right), the other changes $y$ (down–up).

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.7 — Three steps right, four steps up"}
A player stands at $(2, 1)$. The player moves 3 units to the right and 4 units up.

1. Right changes $x$: $2 + 3 = 5$.
2. Up changes $y$: $1 + 4 = 5$.
3. The new position is $(5, 5)$. Both numbers are still plus, so the player is still
   in quadrant I.
4. If the player then moves 7 units to the left: $x = 5 - 7 = -2$. The new position
   $(-2, 5)$ is in quadrant II.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/grid-strike.html" poster="sims/grid-strike.png" title="Grid Strike: hit the coordinates" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build the level in GeoGebra"}
Open the free GeoGebra calculator in a browser (geogebra.org/calculator; no
account is needed).

1. Type the three points of Example 1.5, one per line, for example
   `Coin = (4, 3)`.
2. Add your own enemy in quadrant III and a door on the y-axis.
3. Then play stage 1 of the **Grid Strike** mini-game above.

*Your result:* the coordinates of your enemy and your door, and your Grid
Strike score.
:::

## 1.4 Three-dimensional coordinates

A three-dimensional (3D) world needs a third axis, the **z-axis**, at a right
angle to the other two. A point is now an **ordered triple** $(x, y, z)$: three
numbers in a fixed order (@fig-axes3d).

![The three axes of a 3D world. Here y points up.](images/axes-3d.png){#fig-axes3d width=60%}

In most game engines, $y$ points up. Then:

- $y$ is the **height** above the ground;
- every point on the ground has $y = 0$;
- $x$ and $z$ say where the point is on the ground (right–left and
  forward–back).

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.8 — A drone over the harbour"}
In the 3D version of *Harbor Guard*, a drone is at $(4, 12, -3)$, and $y$ is
up.

1. The height is the middle number: the drone is 12 units above the ground.
2. A tower stands on the ground at $(4, 0, -3)$. The drone is straight above
   the tower: only the height is different.
3. When the drone lands straight down, only $y$ changes, from 12 to 0.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
In C#, the type `Vector3` holds the three numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ of a 3D
position. The letter `f` marks a decimal number.

```csharp
Vector3 drone = new Vector3(4f, 12f, -3f);   // x = 4, y = 12 (height), z = -3
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading the last number as the height. In a world with $y$ up, the height is
the **middle** number.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/position-3d.html" poster="images/axes-3d.png" title="Place an object in 3D" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Move a player in 3D"}
Open the 3D viewer above (or scan its QR code). Drag to turn the world.

1. Move the player to $(1, 2, 4)$ with the sliders. Which slider changes the
   height?
2. Catch three coins. Write the coordinates of each coin.

*Your result:* the slider for the height, and three coordinates $(x, y, z)$.
:::

## 1.5 Left-handed and right-handed systems

When $x$ points right and $y$ points up, the $z$-axis can point *into* the
screen or *out of* it. So there are two kinds of 3D coordinate system. Your
hand tells them apart:

1. point your thumb along $+x$ (right);
2. point your index finger along $+y$ (up);
3. bend your middle finger: it points along $+z$.

If this works with the **left** hand, the system is **left-handed**: $+z$ goes
into the screen. If it works with the **right** hand, the system is
**right-handed**: $+z$ comes out of the screen (@fig-handedness).

![Left-handed (left) and right-handed (right) systems, with x to the right and y up.](images/handedness.png){#fig-handedness width=86%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.4 — Handedness"}
The **handedness** of a 3D coordinate system tells which hand rule its axes
follow: left-handed or right-handed. The two kinds are mirror images of each
other.
:::

Handedness matters because game tools do not agree. A game developer often
uses two tools together (@tbl-conventions).

| Software | Up axis | Handedness |
|---|---|---|
| Unity (game engine) | y | left-handed |
| Blender (3D modelling) | z | right-handed |

: Coordinate systems of two common tools. {#tbl-conventions}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.9 — Which way is up?"}
A designer makes a lamp in Blender and puts it into a Unity game.

1. In Blender, $z$ is up: the height of the lamp is its *last* number.
2. In Unity, $y$ is up: the height is the *middle* number.
3. The export tools change the numbers for us, but the designer must know
   this: if a model appears lying on its side, the up axis is the reason.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that all 3D programs use the same axes. Before you read or type a 3D
position, check which axis is up and which hand rule the program uses.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The hand rule"}
1. Hold your **left** hand in front of the screen: thumb to the right ($+x$),
   index finger up ($+y$). Bend your middle finger. Does it point into the
   screen or towards you?
2. Do the same with your **right** hand.
3. Look at @tbl-conventions. Which hand fits Unity?

*Your result:* "into the screen" or "towards me" for each hand, and the hand
for Unity.
:::

## Case study: where the mathematics is in Harbor Guard

*Harbor Guard* is a made-up tower-defence game for phones. It runs at 60 fps.
The origin of the harbour level is in its centre: the dock is at $(0, -6)$,
the lighthouse at $(-4, 5)$ and the gate at $(3, 2)$. A ship enters at
$(5, 8)$ and sails to the dock. In the 3D version, a drone flies at
$(4, 12, -3)$ with $y$ up, and the towers are made in Blender, where $z$ is
up. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these numbers, and the
mini-game below is a playable version of the harbour: the radar reports a
ship's coordinates, and you build a tower at that point.

{{< sim file="sims/harbor-guard.html" poster="sims/harbor-guard.png" title="Harbor Guard: build towers at the right coordinates" kind="game" height="720" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 1 ("Cartesian Coordinate Systems"): 1D mathematics, 2D and 3D
Cartesian space, and left- and right-handed coordinate spaces.

## Exercises

1. Write the three steps of the game loop.
2. A game runs at 30 fps. How many frames does it make in 10 seconds?
3. Which mathematics does each game task need: (a) the position of a car; (b) the chance of a rare item; (c) "open the door if the player has the
   key"?
4. On a number line, a platform moves from $-2$ to $6$. Write its displacement
   and its distance.
5. A player moves from 5 to 1. Write the displacement and the distance.
6. In which quadrant, or on which axis, is each point: $(-7, 3)$, $(0, -4)$,
   $(5, -1)$, $(-1, -1)$, $(8, 0)$?
7. Write the point 3 units to the right of the centre and 2 units down.
8. In a $y$-up world, a bird is at $(2, 9, 5)$. How high is it?
9. A box is on the ground at $x = 3$ and $z = -1$. Write its 3D position.
10. Use the hand rule: in a left-handed system with $x$ right and $y$ up, does
    $+z$ point into the screen or out of it?
11. Which axis is up in Unity? Which axis is up in Blender?
12. *Harbor Guard*: in which quadrant is the lighthouse $(-4, 5)$? Where is
    the dock $(0, -6)$?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Read the input; change the numbers by the rules; draw the frame.
2. 10 × 30 = 300 frames.
3. (a) coordinates; (b) probability; (c) logic.
4. Displacement 6 − (−2) = 8; distance 8 units.
5. Displacement 1 − 5 = −4; distance 4 units.
6. II; on the y-axis; IV; III; on the x-axis.
7. (3, −2).
8. 9 units (the middle number).
9. (3, 0, −1).
10. Into the screen.
11. Unity: y. Blender: z.
12. The lighthouse is in quadrant II; the dock is on the y-axis (in no quadrant).
:::
